text:
GRU4Rec’s BPR-max directly addresses weak discrimination among high-scoring negatives: softmax weights over negative scores emphasize difficult competitors, avoiding gradient dilution from averaging many easy BPR pairs. Its objective is −log Σj[softmax(r−)j σ(r+−r−j)], with optional negative-score regularization. The authors’ implementation recommends BPR-max or cross-entropy. This remains the strongest family-specific starting point, although the underlying work predates 2023. [GRU4Rec paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf), [official implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)

Recent research supports controlled hardness rather than indiscriminately choosing the hardest items. A 2023 analysis connects hard-negative BPR to partial AUC and top-K ranking, with hardness requiring dataset-specific tuning. Hard-BPR (2024) modifies the objective to reduce false-negative damage under dynamic sampling. Neither establishes gains on this pinned Amazon benchmark. A 2025 sampled-softmax paper also identifies a logQ subtlety: the positive is always included, unlike sampled negatives, so applying the same correction indiscriminately leaves bias. [Hard-negative theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03472), [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276), [LogQ correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)

Experiment implication: compare BPR-max, sampled cross-entropy with correction matched to the actual sampling process, and Hard-BPR as separate single-GRU4Rec trials. Exclude training-known positives from negative pools; tune moderate hardness before aggressive mining. Preserve one checkpoint per category and select exclusively by fixed four-category macro validation HR@10. Improved Electronics training margins alone would not establish better recommendation quality.
